t:
(a) Suits by Prisoners.—Section 7(e) of the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act (42 U.S.C. 1997e(e)) is amended by inserting before the period at the end the following: “or the commission of a sexual act (as defined in section 2246 of title 18, United States Code)”. 
    (b) United States as Defendant.—Section 1346(b)(2) of title 28, United States Code, is amended by inserting before the period at the end the following: “or the commission of a sexual act (as defined in section 2246 of title 18)”. 
    (c) Adoption and Effect of National Standards.—Section 8 of the Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003 (42 U.S.C. 15607) is amended—
        (1) by redesignating subsection (c) as subsection (e); and 
        (2) by inserting after subsection (b) the following:“(c) Applicability to Detention Facilities Operated by the Department of Homeland Security.—“(1) In general.—Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of the Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013, the Secretary of Homeland Security shall publish a final rule adopting national standards for the detection, prevention, reduction, and punishment of rape and sexual assault in facilities that maintain custody of aliens detained for a violation of the immigrations laws of the United States.“(2) Applicability.—The standards adopted under paragraph (1) shall apply to detention facilities operated by the Department of Homeland Security and to detention facilities operated under contract with the Department.“(3) Compliance.—The Secretary of Homeland Security shall—“(A) assess compliance with the standards adopted under paragraph (1) on a regular basis; and“(B) include the results of the assessments in performance evaluations of facilities completed by the Department of Homeland Security.“(4) Considerations.—In adopting standards under paragraph (1), the Secretary of Homeland Security shall give due consideration to the recommended national standards provided by the Commission under section 7(e).“(5) Definition.—As used in this section, the term ‘detention facilities operated under contract with the Department’ includes, but is not limited to contract detention facilities and detention facilities operated through an intergovernmental service agreement with the Department of Homeland Security.“(d) Applicability to Custodial Facilities Operated by the Department of Health and Human Services.—“(1) In general.—Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of the Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013, the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall publish a final rule adopting national standards for the detection, prevention, reduction, and punishment of rape and sexual assault in facilities that maintain custody of unaccompanied alien children (as defined in section 462(g) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 279(g))).“(2) Applicability.—The standards adopted under paragraph (1) shall apply to facilities operated by the Department of Health and Human Services and to facilities operated under contract with the Department.“(3) Compliance.—The Secretary of Health and Human Services shall—“(A) assess compliance with the standards adopted under paragraph (1) on a regular basis; and“(B) include the results of the assessments in performance evaluations of facilities completed by the Department of Health and Human Services.“(4) Considerations.—In adopting standards under paragraph (1), the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall give due consideration to the recommended national standards provided by the Commission under section 7(e).”.

fable.w: The section requires the Secretaries of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services to publish final rules adopting national standards, and required rulemaking counts as participation under the definition. It also directs them to give due consideration to the recommended standards of the Commission under section 7(e). The tempting "No" reading treats subsections (a) and (b) as mere adjustments to the scope of prisoner litigation and the compliance assessments as internal federal activity, but that overlooks the rulemaking mandate.
fable.s: the Secretary of Homeland Security shall publish a final rule adopting national standards for the detection, prevention, reduction, and punishment of rape and sexual assault in facilities that maintain custody of aliens detained for a violation of the immigrations laws of the United States

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act to expand the circumstances under which prisoners can sue the government, specifically adding 'the commission of a sexual act' as a basis for suit. The definition explicitly states that participation includes 'the ability to sue the government over a decision.' Additionally, subsections (c) and (d) require federal Secretaries to 'publish a final rule,' which falls under the definition's inclusion of 'requiring rulemaking.'
qwen_block.s: (a) Suits by Prisoners.—Section 7(e) of the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act (42 U.S.C. 1997e(e)) is amended by inserting before the period at the end the following: “or the commission of a sexual act (as defined in section 2246 of title 18, United States Code)”.
qwen_block.b:
1.  **Think briefly**: The section amends the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act (CRIPA) and the Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA). Subsection (a) amends Section 7(e) of CRIPA, which governs "Suits by Prisoners." By expanding the scope of injuries for which prisoners can sue (adding "sexual act"), it explicitly grants or expands the right of outside parties (prisoners) to sue the government. The definition states: "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision." Subsection (c) and (d) require the Secretaries of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services to publish "final rules" adopting national standards. The definition states: "Answer 'Yes' when the SECTION involves... requiring rulemaking." Rulemaking typically involves public participation (comment periods), and the definition explicitly lists "requiring rulemaking" as a trigger for "Yes". Therefore, the label is "Yes".

opus.w: The section requires the Secretaries of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services to adopt national standards by publishing a final rule. The definition counts required rulemaking as participation, because rulemaking brings in public comment. It also requires them to give due consideration to the standards recommended by the outside Commission. The tempting 'No' reading treats the section as a litigation-limits provision, as subsections (a) and (b) are. But the rulemaking mandate in subsection (c) independently meets the test.
opus.s: the Secretary of Homeland Security shall publish a final rule adopting national standards for the detection, prevention, reduction, and punishment of rape and sexual assault in facilities that maintain custody of aliens detained for a violation of the immigrations laws of the United States.
opus.b:
1. **The tempting wrong reading:** Subsections (a) and (b) are about lawsuits, but they only adjust the limits on prisoner suits and on claims against the United States. Limiting or describing litigation is not the same as granting an outside party a right to sue, so those parts alone would be "No." But the section also directs the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to publish final rules. The definition counts required rulemaking as participation. The Secretaries must also give "due consideration" to standards recommended by the Commission. That is the National Prison Rape Elimination Commission, a body that included non-federal members.

qwen_chat.w: The section explicitly requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to publish a final rule. The definition states that the answer is 'Yes' when the section involves 'requiring rulemaking'. Although the text does not explicitly detail a public comment period, the mandate to issue a final rule falls under the category of requiring rulemaking, which is a specified condition for a 'Yes' label.
qwen_chat.s: the Secretary of Homeland Security shall publish a final rule adopting national standards for the detection, prevention, reduction, and punishment of rape and sexual assault in facilities that maintain custody of aliens detained for a violation of the immigrations laws of the United States
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "giving due consideration" to the Commission's recommendations constitutes participation because it involves an outside entity (the Commission) influencing a federal decision. However, the definition requires that the government *consult or coordinate* with outside parties *before* making a decision. Merely considering recommendations that have already been provided is not the same as an interactive consultation process or a required comment period. Furthermore, the text does not establish the Commission or describe its membership here; it only references standards "provided by the Commission under section 7(e)." The primary action described is the Secretary publishing a final rule. While rulemaking often involves public comment, this specific section mandates the *publication* of the rule and the *consideration* of existing standards, but does not explicitly mandate a public comment period or consultation in this text. More importantly, the "Commission" referenced is likely the National Commission on Correctional Health Care or similar, but without explicit text establishing it as an advisory body with non-federal members *in this section*, and given the passive nature of "give due consideration," it is safer to classify this as "No" unless the text explicitly mandates consultation. Actually, looking closer at the definition: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government...". "Give due consideration" is a weak form of coordination. However, the definition also says "It does not include... applications...". It doesn't explicitly exclude "consideration of recommendations." But the key is "consult or coordinate." Does "give due consideration" equal "consult"? No. Consultation implies a two-way dialogue or seeking input. Considering already provided standards is a one-way receipt of information. Therefore, it is not participation.

Another angle: Does the section *require* rulemaking? Yes, "shall publish a final rule." The definition says: "Answer 'Yes' when the SECTION involves ANY of the following: ... requiring rulemaking". This is a strong indicator. The definition explicitly lists "requiring rulemaking" as a Yes condition. Even if the consultation aspect is weak, the requirement to publish a final rule triggers the "Yes" label under the explicit list of conditions.

Let's re-read the definition carefully: "Answer 'Yes' when the SECTION involves ANY of the following: - requiring a public comment period, or requiring rulemaking;". The section says "the Secretary... shall publish a final rule". This is requiring rulemaking. Therefore, the label is Yes.

Wait, is "publishing a final rule" the same as "requiring rulemaking"? Usually, "requiring rulemaking" implies the statute mandates the agency to go through the rulemaking process (which typically includes notice and comment). The text says "shall publish a final rule". This is a directive to complete the rulemaking process. Thus, it falls under "requiring rulemaking".

Let's double check if there are any traps. "It does not include applications...". This is not an application. "It does include the ability to sue...". Not relevant here. The trap might be that it's just an internal directive. But "requiring rulemaking" is explicitly listed as a Yes.

Let's look at the "tempting-but-wrong" part again. The tempting reading might be "No" because it's just an internal agency action (Secretary publishing a rule). But the definition explicitly includes "requiring rulemaking" as a Yes. So the tempting wrong reading is "No" because it lacks explicit public consultation text. It fails because the definition explicitly lists "requiring rulemaking" as a sufficient condition for "Yes".
